one_liner: Pull-based C23 HTTP/1.1 parser with strict framing checks; beats llhttp on header-heavy messages, not on tiny requests.
what_it_does: A C23 HTTP/1.1 wire parser for requests, responses and standalone header blocks. It fills a typed struct with zero-copy spans: method enum, target, version and up to 64 headers. The API is pull-based: call ihtp_parse_request() on a complete buffer, or call ihtp_parse_request_stateful() repeatedly on one growing buffer. Two optional stages are separate calls: ihtp_request_apply_semantics() resolves framing (body mode, Content-Length, keep-alive, upgrade, Expect, trailers), and ihtp_decode_chunked()/ihtp_decode_fixed() handle the body in place. It is not a drop-in for llhttp's callback API.
how_it_is_fast: The parser core uses block scans instead of llhttp's generated per-byte state machine. libc memchr finds each LF and header colon, and memrchr finds the space before the HTTP version. SWAR checks (8 bytes per 64-bit word, two words per loop iteration) reject control bytes and DEL in request targets and field values. A 256-entry token table is fused with the method/first-space search, methods resolve through a length switch plus memcmp, and results go straight into a caller-owned struct with no allocation or callbacks. The advertised SSE4.2 (PCMPESTRI) and AVX2 scanner is used only for token checks in the semantics layer, and the AVX2 path is a blocked scalar loop, so most of the SIMD comes from libc's memchr.
when_to_use: C servers, proxies or HTTP firewalls on Linux x86-64 that call llhttp today and would prefer a pull API that returns a typed struct of zero-copy header spans.

Header-heavy HTTP/1.1 traffic (about 115-703 byte messages with many or long header values). This is where the benchmark shows 1.15-1.50x over llhttp, e.g. 7.72M vs 5.16M req/s on hdr-value-ascii-clean and 2.89M vs 1.93M on 32 minimal headers.

Security-boundary ingress that needs strict RFC 9112 framing. The strict profile rejects TE+CL, conflicting Content-Length, duplicate or missing Host, bare LF and obs-fold. In the project's chunked-request benchmark the semantics pass adds about 1 ns (130.66 vs 131.74 ns).
Event loops that read into one contiguous, growing buffer and want an explicit resumable parser state plus separate chunked and fixed-length body decoders.
when_not_to_use: When raw parse speed matters and you handle framing yourself: picohttpparser was 1.07-2.46x faster in 21 of the 22 scenarios on the same harness.

Tiny requests and request-line-dominated traffic: llhttp won req-small (49 bytes, 22.91M vs 18.36M req/s, 0.80x), req-line-only, req-line-connect, hdr-name-heavy, hdr-uncommon-valid and hdr-count-04-minimal. Wins on the other request-line cases are 1.01-1.07x, which is within noise on a shared VM.
Callback-driven streaming, ring buffers or scatter I/O: the API needs one contiguous accumulated buffer. Only HTTP/1.0 and 1.1 are parsed, and there is no llhttp-style pause/callback model.
Non-Linux or non-x86 targets, MSVC, or pre-C23 compilers. Only Linux x86-64 is tested, the build turns on -msse4.2/-mavx2 by default, and the code uses GNU memrchr under _GNU_SOURCE.
Anywhere that needs proven maturity: the only release is the pre-release 0.1.0-rc.2, from a single contributor, with 0 stars and no known third-party users or independent benchmark reproductions.

integration.form: static lib (a shared-lib target, CMake package and pkg-config file are also installed; six .c files of about 1.9k lines, small enough to vendor as a source drop)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond a libc that provides memrchr (glibc/musl); CMake 3.25+ to build
integration.min_toolchain: C23 required (CMAKE_C_STANDARD 23; uses nullptr and [[nodiscard]]); CMake 3.25+. Developed and benchmarked with Clang 22.1.0, and GCC presets exist, but the minimum compiler version is not documented.
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 is the only tested platform (CI runs ubuntu-latest with an Oracle Linux 10 dev container). The IOHTTPPARSER_SIMD_SSE42/AVX2 options default ON and add -msse4.2/-mavx2, so other architectures must turn them OFF (inferred from CMakeLists; not documented). macOS and MSVC are not supported as-is because of memrchr and C23.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Parse, semantics and decoder calls touch only caller-owned state and output, so independent parsers on separate threads are fine. The SIMD dispatch table used by the semantics layer is lazily initialized through a plain static bool with no atomic or call_once, which is a formal data race if two threads make the first call at the same time.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false. llhttp is a callback-driven state machine; this is a pull API with typed output structs over a caller-owned accumulated buffer, so the llhttp callback glue has to be rewritten.

gotchas: ihtp_request_t and ihtp_response_t each embed a fixed IHTP_MAX_HEADERS array (default 64, about 2 KB per struct), and the stateless wrappers memset the whole struct on every call. IHTP_MAX_HEADERS changes the struct layout, so the library and every translation unit that includes the headers must be built with the same value. The header comment names a nonexistent -DHP_MAX_HEADERS; the real macro is IHTP_MAX_HEADERS.

The stateful API stores header spans from earlier calls as raw pointers into your accumulated buffer, while its own cursor is only an offset. If you realloc or move that buffer between calls, parsing carries on without error but the earlier spans dangle.
The 'SIMD-accelerated' label mostly does not apply to the parse hot path. ihtp_parse_request/response/headers never call the scanner vtable, so throughput depends largely on your libc's memchr.

IHTP_POLICY_LENIENT relaxes only obs-fold, bare LF, TE+CL and spaces in the request target. The semantics stage still rejects HTTP/1.1 requests without Host, comma-list Content-Length (e.g. '5, 5') and Transfer-Encoding chains that do not end in chunked, and ihtp_decode_chunked() rewrites your buffer in place.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over the picohttpparser-class siblings (the vkrasnov AVX2 fork, hparse, http.c3l) only when you want framing semantics (TE/CL, Host, Connection, upgrade) and a chunked decoder in the same C library; for raw speed those siblings, or plain picohttpparser, win (pico is 1.07-2.46x faster than iohttpparser in 21 of 22 scenarios here). zttp is the llhttp alternative for Python code on httptools; iohttpparser is for C code that calls llhttp directly.
verified_claims_summary: The project's own harness parses one standalone 33-703 byte message per iteration with fresh parser state (200,000 iterations, median of 5 runs). It was built with Clang 22.1.0 (CMake Release + ThinLTO, lld) and run on an 8-vCPU KVM guest that reports only a generic 'AMD EPYC Processor' (host SKU unknown). The best iohttpparser profile (usually stateful-strict) beat vendored llhttp 9.3.1 in 16 of 22 scenarios by 1.01-1.50x and lost the other 6 (down to 0.80x on req-small); llhttp registers no header callbacks in this harness, and framing semantics are not included in these parse-only numbers.
status_note: Pre-release only (v0.1.0-rc.2, 2026-03-14) from a single contributor, with no commits to main since 2026-03-14 (only Dependabot PRs and one maintainer PR open since); dual MIT OR LGPL-2.1-or-later and small enough to vendor on Linux x86-64.
